subject_name: Get Through Mock Exam Paper B

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not associated with increased risk of suicide in patients with cancer?
questions.explanation: Increased risk of suicide in patients with cancer is associated with male gender, advanced stage of disease, poor prognosis, delirium with poor impulse control, poor pain control, depression, hopelessness, history of psychiatric illness, history of previous suicidal attempt, family history of suicide, substance or alcohol abuse, social isolation, advanced age, presence of fatigue and extreme need for control. Patients with cancer have twice the risk of committing suicide as the general population. Hopelessness is even a stronger predictive factor than depression itself. Patients with cancer usually commit suicide by overdosage with analgesics or sedative drugs prescribed by their doctors. Men use violent means, such as hanging or gunshot, more often than women.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about first-rank and second-rank symptoms is incorrect?

options.text: First-rank symptoms include auditory hallucinations that are in the third person.
First-rank symptoms include delusions such as made feelings, impulses and actions.
First-rank symptoms are pathognomonic of schizophrenia.

correct_answer.text: First-rank symptoms are pathognomonic of schizophrenia.

correct_answers.text: First-rank symptoms are pathognomonic of schizophrenia.

questions.explanation: The classical first-rank symptoms include auditory hallucinations (repeating the thoughts out loud, in third person, in the form of a running commentary), delusions of passivity (thought insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting and made feelings, impulses and actions) and somatic passivity. Second-rank symptoms include perplexity, emotional blunting. It should be noted that first-rank symptoms could occur in other psychoses and, although highly suggestive of schizophrenia, are not pathognomonic of the condition.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a psychiatric feature of Smith–Magenis syndrome?
questions.explanation: Smith–Magenis syndrome is caused by the complete or partial deletion of chromosome 17p11.2. Its psychiatric features include schizophrenia-like psychosis, inappropriate affect, aggression, sleep disturbances and self-harming behaviour. Other clinical features include hearing problems, hoarse and deep voice, renal problems, inguinal/umbilical hernia, hypospadias (in 10% of male patients), short broad hands and small toes, hypotonia, hyperextensible fingers and moderate-to-severe learning disability.

questions.question_text: Which of the following parameters on the Violence Risk Appraisal Guide (VRAG) has the strongest correlation with violent recidivism?

options.text: Separated from parents before age of 16 years

questions.explanation: The Violence Risk Appraisal Guide (VRAG) is an actuarial violence risk assessment that is entirely reliant on historical factors. It is made up of 12 items and includes PCL-R as a subscale. The strongest correlate with violent recidivism is the PCL-R score with a positive correlation equivalent to explaining approximately 10% of the variance in violent reoffending.

questions.question_text: What is the increase in risk of a 17-year-old male adolescent of acquiring alcohol disorder if his father has been diagnosed with chronic alcoholism?
questions.explanation: There is an estimated fourfold increase in risk of alcohol dependency in first-degree relatives of alcoholics. Adopted children of alcoholic parents have the same fourfold increased risk of alcohol dependency as children raised by their alcohol-dependent parents.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old woman is concerned about developing dementia and consults you on supplementation that she can use to prevent dementia. Which of the following medications or supplements would you recommend?

options.text: Do not recommend any of the above.

correct_answer.text: Do not recommend any of the above.

correct_answers.text: Do not recommend any of the above.

questions.explanation: The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines advise not to use the above drugs as specific treatment for the primary prevention of dementia.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man, who was treated by his psychiatrist for alcohol dependence, is brought in to the emergency department for drunk driving and rowdy behaviour. He denies drinking alcohol and claims that he has abstained from alcohol for the past 6 months. Which of the following tests would you perform to confirm that he is drinking again?
questions.explanation: GGT becomes elevated after acute or chronic alcohol use and remains elevated for 2–5 weeks afterwards. It is commonly used as an objective indicator of relapse.

questions.question_text: A researcher wants to know the prevalence of various psychiatric illnesses in the country. He selects a representative sample and surveys them about their psychiatric history. What type of study is this?
questions.explanation: Cross-sectional studies analyse a population (or a representative subset) at a single point in time and are used to assess disease prevalence. All variables are measured at the same time.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a measure of internal validity of a randomized controlled trial (RCT)?
questions.explanation: Internal validity is the extent to which the results of a study are true and not caused by extraneous factors. Sample size computation relates to power and external validity rather than internal validity.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding meta-analysis is false?

options.text: Combining results of RCTs and open-label trials in one forest plot is appropriate.
Publication bias may skew results because of the tendency to publish studies with positive results.
Meta-analysis offers greater precision as a result of larger sample size.

The Cochrane Collaboration produces and disseminates systematic reviews of healthcare interventions and promotes the search for evidence in the form of clinical trials and other studies of the effects of interventions.
Systematic review of RCTs is level 1A evidence.

correct_answer.text: Combining results of RCTs and open-label trials in one forest plot is appropriate.

correct_answers.text: Combining results of RCTs and open-label trials in one forest plot is appropriate.

questions.explanation: Meta-analysis is a collection of techniques whereby the results of two or more independent studies are statistically combined to yield an overall estimate. It is not appropriate to combine RCTs and open-label trials in the same forest plot.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medical complications is not routinely associated with anorexia nervosa?
questions.explanation: Growth hormone is increased in patients suffering from anorexia nervosa. Bone mineral density is reduced; leukopenia, mitral valve prolapse and pancreatitis can occur in patients with anorexia nervosa.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old shopkeeper presented to the Accident and Emergency Department with memory loss. Which of the following features do not suggest transient global amnesia?

options.text: He cannot remember the events that occurred in the afternoon.
He cannot recall the name of his shop.
He is disorientated in time and place.
He demonstrates anterograde amnesia after admission to the ward.
He demonstrates retrograde amnesia for variable durations.

correct_answer.text: He demonstrates anterograde amnesia after admission to the ward.

correct_answers.text: He demonstrates anterograde amnesia after admission to the ward.

questions.explanation: Transient global amnesia usually lasts for a few hours and seldom recurs. It will not lead to anterograde amnesia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding narcolepsy is false?

options.text: Genotype HLA-DQB1*0602 is present in nearly 99% of people suffering from narcolepsy.
Hypnopompic hallucinations are commoner than hypnagogic hallucination.
Loss of hypocretin cells in the hypothalamus is an aetiological factor.
Modafinil is useful to treat this condition.
Nocturnal sleep polysomnography shows rapid eye movement (REM) sleep latency less than or equal to 15 min.

correct_answer.text: Hypnopompic hallucinations are commoner than hypnagogic hallucination.

correct_answers.text: Hypnopompic hallucinations are commoner than hypnagogic hallucination.

questions.explanation: Hypnagogic hallucinations occur in 20%–40% of individuals. They are usually visual or dream-like. Hypnopompic hallucinations are less common compared with hypnagogic hallucinations.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man presents with rapidly progressive dementia plus pyramidal and extrapyramidal deficits, preceded by a brief period of anxiety and depression. Which disorder is he likely to be suffering from?
questions.explanation: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease is a rare cause of rapidly progressive dementia. There may be a brief prodrome of anxiety or depression. Sudden onset and rapid progression with pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs are typical.

questions.question_text: A 72-year-old woman with a background of cerebrovascular accident 2 years ago presents with seizures. Which of the following statements regarding seizures in the elderly is false?

options.text: A high percentage of people with seizure may have normal electroencephalogram (EEG) findings.
Alzheimer’s disease dementia is not a risk factor for refractory seizures.
Strokes or tumours are common causes of seizures in the elderly.
The incidence of seizures is high.

correct_answer.text: Alzheimer’s disease dementia is not a risk factor for refractory seizures.

correct_answers.text: Alzheimer’s disease dementia is not a risk factor for refractory seizures.

questions.explanation: Alzheimer’s disease is a risk factor for refractory seizures in the elderly. Strokes or tumours account for about half of cases, and up to 80% of seizures in the elderly become recurrent.

questions.question_text: Based on previous studies, the diagnosis of very-late-onset psychosis should be made only if the individual is above which age?
questions.explanation: Very-late-onset psychosis (paraphrenia) is defined by onset after 60 years of age, with well-organized delusions and preserved personality.

questions.question_text: A 42-year-old woman says that she has repeated thoughts that her table is dirty and she has to snap her fingers five times to dispel these thoughts. Which one of the following defence mechanisms is this?
questions.explanation: Undoing is an attempt to negate an unacceptable thought or act by performing a counteracting behaviour. It is common in obsessive–compulsive disorder.

questions.question_text: Which of the following defence mechanisms is most often seen in people with phobias?
questions.explanation: In phobias, patients often isolate the fear from conscious awareness and displace it onto an external object.

questions.question_text: For an antipsychotic to be effective, it has to achieve what percentage blockage of the dopaminergic receptors?
questions.explanation: Neuroimaging studies suggest that approximately 65%–78% dopamine receptor blockade is required for optimal antipsychotic efficacy with minimal side effects.

questions.question_text: The male-to-female gender ratio for conduct disorder is which of the following?
questions.explanation: Epidemiological data show a male-to-female ratio of about 3:1 for conduct disorder.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most common neuropsychiatric disorder in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)?
questions.explanation: Cognitive dysfunction affects up to 80% of patients with neuropsychiatric lupus and is the most common manifestation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following assessment toolkits best predicts the needs for support services for an elderly patient with dementia?

options.text: Clifton assessment procedures for the elderly

correct_answer.text: Clifton assessment procedures for the elderly

correct_answers.text: Clifton assessment procedures for the elderly

questions.explanation: The Clifton assessment procedures for the elderly (CAPE) assesses disability level and predicts needs for support services in dementia care.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man with HIV/AIDS on ward for 6 weeks develops low mood and loss of interest. Which of the following antidepressants is better to be avoided?
questions.explanation: Bupropion lowers seizure threshold and is contraindicated in patients with advanced HIV, epilepsy or HIV-related dementia.

questions.question_text: Effects of antipsychotics on which receptor would have resulted in his current symptoms of sexual dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Antagonism at 5-HT2A receptors is associated with sexual dysfunction in patients on antipsychotics.

questions.question_text: Regarding the course of illness for autistic disorder, which of the following symptoms do not improve across time?
questions.explanation: Restricted, stereotyped and repetitive behaviours in autism tend to persist over time, whereas social and communication deficits may improve.

questions.question_text: An 11-year-old child referred for new-onset nocturnal enuresis. Which of the following has not been found to be associated with nocturnal enuresis?
questions.explanation: Nocturnal enuresis is more commonly associated with short stature. A positive family history, neurological signs and recurrence after medication withdrawal are common associations.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding the impact of divorce on children is incorrect?

options.text: Children of divorced parents are sexually active at a younger age.
If the mother remarries, her son has a better relationship with the step-father compared with her daughter.
The mother–daughter bond is more affected than the mother–son bond if the mother remarries.
Divorce causes more anxiety in children than parental death.
On average, girls are more distressed than boys by the divorce.

correct_answer.text: On average, girls are more distressed than boys by the divorce.

correct_answers.text: On average, girls are more distressed than boys by the divorce.

questions.explanation: On average, boys are more distressed than girls by divorce, although girls may react more to maternal remarriage.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding reading disorder is incorrect?

options.text: The prevalence of dyslexia in the United Kingdom is 5%.
The prevalence of genuine dyslexia and mild dyslexia is 10%.
In the United States, 17%–20% of elementary school children are estimated to suffer from reading disabilities.
In the United States, 17%–20% of the population display a reading disability.

A survey conducted across Japan, Taiwan and the United States concluded that using more than one criterion, the percentage of children who were reading disabled were 8% in Japan, 8% in Taiwan and 7% in the United States.

correct_answer.text: In the United States, 17%–20% of the population display a reading disability.

correct_answers.text: In the United States, 17%–20% of the population display a reading disability.

questions.explanation: The true prevalence of reading disability in the general population is around 2%–8%, not 17%–20%.

questions.question_text: In which domains on the MMPI would a bulimic patient have elevated scores compared with anorexics?
questions.explanation: Compared with anorexics, bulimics score higher on measures of neuroticism and psychoticism, reflecting greater mood lability and impulsivity.

questions.question_text: Which of the following offences is the most common first presentation of conduct disorder?
questions.explanation: Shoplifting or stealing objects of value is the most common initial offending behaviour in conduct disorder.

questions.question_text: All the following statements about suicide in the elderly are true, with the exception of which?

options.text: Males tend to have a higher rate of suicide compared with females, using more lethal methods.
Presence of hopelessness, guilt, insomnia and delusions of guilt predispose to suicide.
Individuals are at enhanced risk if they suffer a recent loss or during anniversaries.
Individuals are at enhanced risk in the first few weeks after the commencement of antidepressant therapy.
Most elderly individuals who have committed suicide tend not to have sought consultation prior to their act.

correct_answer.text: Most elderly individuals who have committed suicide tend not to have sought consultation prior to their act.

correct_answers.text: Most elderly individuals who have committed suicide tend not to have sought consultation prior to their act.

questions.explanation: This is incorrect. About 80% of elderly individuals who complete suicide have seen their general practitioner in the months before their death.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about aging and its effects on memory is incorrect?

options.text: Short-term memory as tested by digit span does not change with age.
Memory tasks requiring monitoring or complex decision making are usually performed more poorly in the elderly.
Retrieval of information in the elderly is impaired, and in particular, cued recall is affected.
Older subjects tend to be less likely to code at the semantic level for memories.
Memory performance is best if the meaning is easily extracted.

correct_answer.text: Retrieval of information in the elderly is impaired, and in particular, cued recall is affected.

correct_answers.text: Retrieval of information in the elderly is impaired, and in particular, cued recall is affected.

questions.explanation: This is incorrect: un-cued (free) recall is more affected by age than is cued recall.

questions.question_text: Approximately what percentage of patients with late-onset psychosis have at least one first-rank symptom?
questions.explanation: About 46% of individuals with late-onset psychosis exhibit at least one Schneiderian first-rank symptom.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old patient with schizophrenia and Gilles de la Tourette’s syndrome: Which feature is most suggestive of Tourette’s syndrome?
questions.explanation: Tics, characterized by sudden, rapid, involuntary purposeless movements, are the hallmark of Tourette’s syndrome.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not an example of objective personality measure?
questions.explanation:
Objective	personality	measures	involve	the	scoring	of	individual	responses,	by	an	observer
based	on	a	user	manual	and	instructions.	This	includes	Million	Behavioural	Health	Inventory	(MBHI),
Million	Clinical	Multiaxial	Inventory	(MCMI),	PAI	and	MMPI.	Projective	personality	measures	involve
the	eliciting	of	responses	that	allow	psychodiagnostic	interference	and	detect	disorders	of	reality	testing
and	thought	processes;	this	includes	Rorschach	Inkblot	Test	(RIT)	and	the	thematic	apperception	test
(TAT)

questions.question_text: Which of the following measures is not part of the Halstead–Reitan Neuropsychological Test Battery (HRNTB)?
questions.explanation: The HRNTB consists of input measures, abstraction tests, sensory input, and output measures. It does not include a specific verbal abilities subtest.

questions.question_text: Which of the following neurotransmitters is least likely to be involved in the modulation of aggression?
questions.explanation: Aggression is modulated by catecholamines (adrenaline, noradrenaline), dopamine and serotonin. Acetylcholine is not implicated.

questions.question_text: With regard to enuresis and encopresis, which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.text: Seventy percent of enuresis is caused by organic causes.
Regressive encopresis is associated with a good prognosis.
Encopresis is associated with aggression and a short attention span.
Diurnal enuresis is more common in females.
If a child presents with both enuresis and encopresis, enuresis should be treated first.

correct_answer.text: If a child presents with both enuresis and encopresis, enuresis should be treated first.

correct_answers.text: If a child presents with both enuresis and encopresis, enuresis should be treated first.

questions.explanation: In combined cases, encopresis should be treated before enuresis. Aggressive encopresis carries a poorer prognosis, and diurnal enuresis is more common in females due to higher UTI risk.

questions.question_text: Which of the following regarding the water deprivation test is false?

options.text: In normal subjects, urine osmolality rises as urine volume falls.
In patients with cranial diabetes insipidus, urine osmolality fails to rise despite increasing plasma osmolality.
In patients with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, the urine concentrates normally in response to desmopressin.
With primary polydipsia, excessive fluid intake prior may result in continued diuresis despite fluid restriction.
With primary polydipsia, plasma osmolality remains below 295 mosmol/kg after fluid restriction.

correct_answer.text: In patients with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, the urine concentrates normally in response to desmopressin.

correct_answers.text: In patients with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, the urine concentrates normally in response to desmopressin.

questions.explanation: In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, the kidneys cannot respond to desmopressin and thus fail to concentrate urine.

questions.question_text: You have designed a research project that investigates the effects of three different antipsychotics on the metabolic syndrome. Which statistical test would you use?
questions.explanation: ANOVA is used to compare means across three or more groups when the data are normally distributed.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is the correct definition of type one error?

options.text: The probability that the false null hypothesis will be rejected.
The probability of accepting the null hypothesis when it is false.
The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true.
The probability that the study lacks power.
The probability that the null hypothesis will be accepted.

correct_answer.text: The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true.

correct_answers.text: The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true.

questions.explanation: A type one error (α) is rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true (false positive).

questions.question_text: Upon the release of a new antidepressant, you compare the proportion of patients who develop gastric side effects with those using fluoxetine. Which test do you use?
questions.explanation: The chi-square test compares categorical outcomes (side effect present/absent) between independent groups.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most likely to increase response rates for mailed questionnaires?

options.text: Conducting face-to-face interviews at the participants’ homes

questions.explanation: Monetary incentives have been shown to significantly improve response rates to mailed surveys.

questions.question_text: What is the primary mechanism of action of cocaine?

options.text: It blocks activity of monoamine oxidase.
It causes release of dopamine into synapses.

questions.explanation: Cocaine competitively inhibits the dopamine transporter, blocking dopamine reuptake and increasing synaptic dopamine.

questions.question_text: Which medication commonly used in alcohol dependence works via inhibition of a critical step in the breakdown of alcohol?
questions.explanation: Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing acetaldehyde buildup and unpleasant reactions if alcohol is consumed.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a serious side effect of 3,4-methylenedioxy-N-methylamphetamine (MDMA)?
questions.explanation: MDMA can cause lethal hyperthermia mediated by serotoninergic overactivity.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a symptom of cocaine withdrawal?
questions.explanation: Appetite is usually increased, not decreased, during cocaine withdrawal.

questions.question_text: What percentage of people convicted of homicide in England and Wales were assessed to have abnormal mental state at the time of the offence?
questions.explanation: Approximately 10% of homicide offenders were judged to have been mentally ill at the time of the offence.

questions.question_text: Which personality disorder is most common in female prisoners in England?
questions.explanation: Antisocial personality disorder is the most prevalent diagnosis among female prisoners.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding the HCR-20 is false?

options.text: It does not consider protective factors in the assessment.
It does not require formal training.
It focuses on violence towards people and property.
It cannot be used to measure dangerousness.

correct_answer.text: It focuses on violence towards people and property.

correct_answers.text: It focuses on violence towards people and property.

questions.explanation: The HCR-20 focuses on violence towards people; it does not assess property violence or animal violence.

questions.question_text: Which of the following environmental factors is not a risk factor for inpatient violence?
questions.explanation: High levels of staff–patient interaction are protective. Risk factors include lack of privacy, overcrowding, poor facilities and frequent use of agency staff.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false regarding homocystinuria?

options.text: Administration of vitamin B6 facilitates metabolism of homocysteine and reduces levels of homocysteine and methionine.
Elevated serum homocysteine level is a risk factor for stroke.
It is attributed to mutation on chromosome 22.
Patients have mental retardation, personality disorders and obsessive-compulsive symptoms.
There is malformation of multiple organs.

correct_answer.text: It is attributed to mutation on chromosome 22.

correct_answers.text: It is attributed to mutation on chromosome 22.

questions.explanation: Homocystinuria is due to a mutation in the CBS gene on chromosome 21, not 22.

questions.question_text: A 4-year-old with gaze aversion, long face, large ears, enlarged testes, flat feet, IQ of 60 and hand flapping. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability. Features include macroorchidism, long face, large ears, flat feet and autistic behaviours.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most common cause of mental retardation?
questions.explanation: In about one-third of cases no specific cause is identified (idiopathic). This category is the most common overall.

questions.question_text: A 5-year-old boy presents with autism. Which of the following is false?

options.text: There is a tendency to echolalia and pronoun reversal.
Stimulants can relieve the stereotyped behaviours.
IQ is the most important prognostic factor.
He may suffer from fragile X syndrome or tuberous sclerosis.

correct_answer.text: Stimulants can relieve the stereotyped behaviours.

correct_answers.text: Stimulants can relieve the stereotyped behaviours.

questions.explanation: Stimulants may reduce hyperactivity in autistic children but do not relieve stereotyped behaviours.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old female student with bulimia requests psychotherapy. The most appropriate choice is:
questions.explanation: Interpersonal psychotherapy and cognitive–behavioural therapy are both evidence-based treatments for bulimia nervosa.

questions.question_text: Paranoid schizophrenics are how many times more likely to commit suicide compared with non-paranoid individuals?
questions.explanation: Paranoid schizophrenia carries about a threefold higher suicide risk compared with non-paranoid cases.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old woman with bulimia and major depression. Which antidepressant is contraindicated?
questions.explanation: Bupropion is associated with an increased risk of seizures in patients with eating disorders and is contraindicated.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man with vascular changes and enlarged ventricles on CT. Which clinical sign should be expected?
questions.explanation: Binswanger’s disease (subcortical vascular dementia) commonly produces pseudobulbar palsy, gait disturbance and urinary incontinence.

questions.question_text: A 72-year-old Alzheimer’s patient with behavioural symptoms. The therapist uses the "here and now" meaning-focused approach. Which therapy is this?
questions.explanation: Resolution therapy focuses on the “here and now” behaviour meanings as a companion technique to reality orientation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a characteristic neurotransmitter change in Alzheimer’s dementia?
questions.explanation: The main neurotransmitter abnormality is loss of cholinergic neurons in the basal forebrain, leading to low cortical cholinergic activity and reduced choline acetyl-transferase. Dopamine and noradrenaline are also decreased; serotonin is not increased.

questions.question_text: Which of the following factors is not associated with higher rates of panic disorder among people seeking treatment for chest pain in emergency rooms?
questions.explanation: Studies show panic disorder is more likely with atypical pain, female gender, younger age and high anxiety, but it is less common in those with established coronary artery disease.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding hypochondriasis is false?

options.text: It is associated with lower socio-economic status and a history of medical illness.
Onset is most common in early adulthood.
The presence of comorbid medical illness is a poor prognostic factor.
Somatization disorder is a common comorbid diagnosis.

correct_answer.text: The presence of comorbid medical illness is a poor prognostic factor.

correct_answers.text: The presence of comorbid medical illness is a poor prognostic factor.

questions.explanation: The presence of a comorbid medical illness is actually a good prognostic factor in hypochondriasis, not a poor one.

questions.question_text: A 74-year-old woman with delusional parasitosis insists worms crawl under her skin. Which statement is true regarding her condition?

options.text: Antidepressants are helpful to remove the ruminations.
Patients are usually keen for psychiatric consultation.
Patients typically have experienced an actual infestation or exposure to organisms in the past.
Patients are usually keen to receive psychiatric treatment as they have retained insight into their condition.
There is usually no specific precipitating event.

correct_answer.text: Patients typically have experienced an actual infestation or exposure to organisms in the past.

correct_answers.text: Patients typically have experienced an actual infestation or exposure to organisms in the past.

questions.explanation: Many patients with delusional parasitosis report a past actual infestation or exposure, and they are usually reluctant for psychiatric referral.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a common comorbid psychiatric disorder of patients suffering from trichotillomania?
questions.explanation: Common comorbidities with trichotillomania include anxiety, depression, substance abuse and eating disorders. No specific personality disorder is characteristic.

questions.question_text: Which of the following mood stabilizers would you least likely consider in a patient who is concerned about cognitive side effects?
questions.explanation: Topiramate has the highest risk of cognitive side effects (verbal fluency decline, slowed reaction time) among mood stabilizers.

questions.question_text: Referring to Table 3.1, which of the following best describes the above study?
questions.explanation: The study measures direct and indirect costs against clinical outcomes (e.g. HAMD scores), making it a cost-effectiveness analysis.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not considered to be a direct cost related to depressive disorder?

options.text: Cost of consultation with GP related to depressive disorder
Cost of hospitalization related to depressive disorder
Cost of psychotherapy to treat depression
Cost of sick leave related to depressive disorder
Cost of thyroid function tests to rule out underlying organic cause for depression

correct_answer.text: Cost of sick leave related to depressive disorder

correct_answers.text: Cost of sick leave related to depressive disorder

questions.explanation: Cost of sick leave represents lost productivity and is therefore an indirect cost, not a direct healthcare cost.

questions.question_text: Referring to Table 3.2, which of the following factors is the most important predictor of indirect cost for depressive disorder in Singapore?

options.text: Number of suicide attempts in 1 year

questions.explanation: In multivariate regression, the mean Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD) score over one year remained the strongest predictor of indirect costs.

questions.question_text: Based on Table 3.3, which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.text: The higher scores on the DFIQ correlate with poorer HRQOL in the children, and the correlation is significant.
The higher scores on the DFIQ correlate with poorer physical health (SF-12 PH) and mental health (SF-12 MH). The correlations are significant.
The later age of onset correlates with better mental health, and the correlation is significant.
The severity of atopic dermatitis (SCORAD) correlates with older age of the child, and the correlation is significant.
The severity of atopic dermatitis (SCORAD) correlates with poorer physical health (SF-12 PH), and the correlation is significant.

correct_answer.text: The higher scores on the DFIQ correlate with poorer HRQOL in the children, and the correlation is significant.

correct_answers.text: The higher scores on the DFIQ correlate with poorer HRQOL in the children, and the correlation is significant.

questions.explanation: The reported correlation between DFIQ and HRQOL is positive (higher DFIQ with higher HRQOL scores), which indicates better HRQOL, not poorer.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man with long-standing substance abuse presents with cognitive impairment. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Chronic inhalant use can cause irreversible cognitive impairment, cerebellar dysfunction and peripheral neuropathy.

questions.question_text: Henry, a 40-year-old alcoholic for 20 years, asks the risk for his 14-year-old adopted son developing alcohol dependence. What do you tell him?
questions.explanation: First-degree relatives have about a fourfold increased risk of alcohol dependence, even if adopted into a non-drinking family.

questions.question_text: During an inhalant use episode, which of the following leads to the greatest risk of death?

options.text: Burns to the throat and lungs
Persistent cerebellar syndrome and peripheral neuropathy

questions.explanation: Sudden sniffing death syndrome from cardiac arrhythmias is the greatest acute risk with inhalant abuse.

questions.question_text: A drug dealer with haematuria, difficulty passing urine, incoherence and violence. Which illicit substance?
questions.explanation: Ketamine misuse can cause severe lower urinary tract symptoms, haematuria and dysuria.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old woman with tachycardia, confusion and closeness to others after party pills. Intoxication from:
questions.explanation: Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) causes tachycardia, euphoria, feelings of empathy and possible hyperthermia.

questions.question_text: What is the lifetime prevalence rate of schizophrenia in all perpetrators of homicide?
questions.explanation: About 5% of homicide perpetrators have schizophrenia at some point in their lives.

questions.question_text: First-episode psychosis: what percentage eventually have schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Approximately 35% of first-episode psychosis patients are later diagnosed with schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the strongest predictor of sexual recidivism?

options.text: Three previous convictions for sexual offending
Young age of first sexual offence conviction

correct_answer.text: Young age of first sexual offence conviction

correct_answers.text: Young age of first sexual offence conviction

questions.explanation: A history of multiple prior sexual offence convictions is the strongest static predictor of sexual recidivism.

questions.question_text: A 24-year-old man diagnosed with Klinefelter syndrome. Which best describes the inheritance pattern?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) usually occurs sporadically from nondisjunction events; it is not inherited.

questions.question_text: Adults with Down syndrome are not at increased risk of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Down syndrome is associated with early-onset Alzheimer’s dementia but not vascular dementia.

questions.question_text: Cri du chat syndrome is a deletion of 5p. Which is not characteristic of this condition?
questions.explanation: Cri du chat causes severe intellectual disability and motor delay, not moderate mental retardation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true regarding fragile X syndrome?

options.text: Symptoms tend to be much more severe in females than in males.
It occurs secondary to mutations in the fragile mental retardation 2 (FMR2) gene.
It occurs in expansion of CGG trinucleotide repeats of over 200 triplets.
There is atrophy of the caudate nucleus and hippocampus.
Those with permutations are not at risk of developing fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS).

correct_answer.text: It occurs in expansion of CGG trinucleotide repeats of over 200 triplets.

correct_answers.text: It occurs in expansion of CGG trinucleotide repeats of over 200 triplets.

questions.explanation: Fragile X full mutation involves >200 CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene; permutations (55–200 repeats) do carry FXTAS risk.

questions.question_text: Somnambulism leading to non-consensual acts: concerning the defence of "not guilty by reason of insanity," which is true?

options.text: Somnambulism is classified as sane automatism.
Somnambulism is classified as insane automatism.
There is a fixed maximum punishment for legal automatisms.
Voluntary intoxication with alcohol is classified as sane automatism.
Voluntary intoxication with alcohol is classified as insane automatism.

correct_answer.text: Somnambulism is classified as insane automatism.

correct_answers.text: Somnambulism is classified as insane automatism.

questions.explanation: Somnambulism (sleepwalking) is considered a product of mental disease and is classified as insane automatism.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding melatonin is incorrect?

options.text: If an adolescent takes melatonin and the oral contraceptive pill concurrently, melatonin has less propensity to cause drug interactions.
A prolonged-release formulation of melatonin is licensed for the short-term treatment of insomnia in children in the United Kingdom.
Meta-analyses of small RCTs comparing melatonin with placebo in children with insomnia show consistent improvement in sleep.
Melatonin can worsen asthma and seizure in the short term.
The optimal dose of melatonin in the treatment of insomnia in children and adolescents is unknown.

correct_answer.text: A prolonged-release formulation of melatonin is licensed for the short-term treatment of insomnia in children in the United Kingdom.

correct_answers.text: A prolonged-release formulation of melatonin is licensed for the short-term treatment of insomnia in children in the United Kingdom.

questions.explanation: A prolonged-release melatonin is licensed for short-term use in adults over 55, not in children.

questions.question_text: An advanced practice nurse wants a structured interview for substance misuse and psychiatric disorders. Which would you recommend?

options.text: Chemical Use, Abuse and Dependence (CUAD) survey
Inventory of Substance Abuse Treatment Services (SATS)
Psychiatric Research Interview for Substance and Mental Disorders (PRISM)
Stages of Change Readiness and Treatment Eagerness Scale (SOCRATES)

correct_answer.text: Psychiatric Research Interview for Substance and Mental Disorders (PRISM)

correct_answers.text: Psychiatric Research Interview for Substance and Mental Disorders (PRISM)

questions.explanation: PRISM is a structured diagnostic interview designed to assess both substance use disorders and comorbid psychiatric diagnoses.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false regarding the General Health Questionnaire (GHQ)?

options.text: It primarily identifies non-psychotic psychiatric illness and assesses its severity.
It focuses on functioning over the past 2 weeks.
It uses a four-point scale ranging from ‘much more than usual’ to ‘less than usual’.

correct_answer.text: It focuses on functioning over the past 2 weeks.

correct_answers.text: It focuses on functioning over the past 2 weeks.

questions.explanation: The GHQ focuses on functioning over the past month, not just two weeks.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true about the Montgomery and Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS)?

options.text: It is not a sensitive measure of change in symptom severity during treatment.
It is useful for people with concurrent physical illness, as it places less emphasis on somatic symptoms.
A score of 7–25 is indicative of mild depression.
It cannot be used for assessing patients who are likely to experience side effects from medication.

correct_answer.text: It is useful for people with concurrent physical illness, as it places less emphasis on somatic symptoms.

correct_answers.text: It is useful for people with concurrent physical illness, as it places less emphasis on somatic symptoms.

questions.explanation: MADRS de-emphasizes somatic symptoms, making it useful in patients with physical comorbidity.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false regarding the Hamilton Depression Scale?

options.text: It assesses symptoms in the last 7 days.
It monitors changes in the severity of the symptoms during treatment.
It should only be used on patients with an established diagnosis of depression, as it is not a diagnostic instrument.
Its validity is affected if the person has concurrent physical illness.
One of its strengths is that behavioural symptoms and somatic complaints are preferred over self-reported distress.

correct_answer.text: One of its strengths is that behavioural symptoms and somatic complaints are preferred over self-reported distress.

correct_answers.text: One of its strengths is that behavioural symptoms and somatic complaints are preferred over self-reported distress.

questions.explanation: While behavioural and somatic items are included, this is a criticism rather than a recognized strength; its validity is affected by physical illness.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding differences between parametric and non-parametric tests is correct?

options.text: ANOVA is used for non-parametric data.
Mann–Whitney U is used for parametric data.
Non-parametric data follows a normal distribution but not for parametric data.
Sample size for parametric data is preferably >30, but for non-parametric, it is best for <50 data cases.
The confidence interval calculation for parametric data is more difficult than for non-parametric data.

correct_answer.text: Sample size for parametric data is preferably >30, but for non-parametric, it is best for <50 data cases.

correct_answers.text: Sample size for parametric data is preferably >30, but for non-parametric, it is best for <50 data cases.

questions.explanation: Parametric tests assume normal distribution and typically require larger sample sizes (n>30); non-parametric tests are used with smaller or skewed samples.

questions.question_text: Which statistical test would you use for measuring differences in education level among different ethnic groups (Caucasians, African Caribbean, Southern and Eastern Asians)?
questions.explanation: Education level categories and ethnicity form a contingency table; the chi-square test compares proportions across these groups.

questions.question_text: Which statistical method is used for correlation analysis in ranked or skewed data?
questions.explanation: Spearman correlation assesses monotonic relationships between ranked or non-normally distributed variables.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false for confidence interval (CI)?

options.text: A 99% CI is wider than a 95% CI.
A 95% CI means that one is 95% confident that the interval contains the true population mean.
For relative risk or odds ratio, if the CI contains 1, then the results are not different.
The CI is the interval that true statistics believes to be found within a given population with a known probability.
Width of the CI is dependent on sample size: a larger sample generates wider CI.

correct_answer.text: Width of the CI is dependent on sample size: a larger sample generates wider CI.

correct_answers.text: Width of the CI is dependent on sample size: a larger sample generates wider CI.

questions.explanation: A larger sample size generates a narrower, not wider, confidence interval.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding hoarding is false?

options.text: Hoarding is most commonly found in people with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).
It shows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.
There is lower activity in the dorsal anterior cingulate gyrus and occipital cortex of people with hoarding and OCD.
Treatment involves selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs).

correct_answer.text: It shows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.

correct_answers.text: It shows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.

questions.explanation: Hoarding symptoms have been linked to autosomal recessive patterns and loci on chromosomes 4, 5 and 17, not dominant inheritance.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding immune function in depressed patients is false?

options.text: A syndrome of ‘sickness behaviour’ that resembles major depression can occur with the administration of interferons.
Peripheral blood shows decreased lymphocyte number and increased neutrophil number.
There are decreased levels of interleukin (IL)-6 and IL-1-beta.
There are increased acute phase proteins.
There is increased level of tumour necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha compared with non-depressed individuals.

correct_answer.text: There are decreased levels of interleukin (IL)-6 and IL-1-beta.

correct_answers.text: There are decreased levels of interleukin (IL)-6 and IL-1-beta.

questions.explanation: Depressed patients have elevated, not decreased, levels of IL-6 and IL-1-beta in peripheral blood and CSF.

questions.question_text: Based on the P50 auditory-evoked potential, which chromosome is implicated in the failure of sensory gating phenomenon in schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Failure of P50 sensory gating in schizophrenia has been linked to the alpha-7 nicotinic receptor gene on chromosome 15.

questions.question_text: Long-term risperidone (oral + depot) leading to elevated prolactin: what percentage of D2 blockade is associated with this?
questions.explanation: Approximately 72% dopamine D2 receptor occupancy is required to induce hyperprolactinemia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a common biological abnormality shared by both schizophrenia and schizotypal disorder?
questions.explanation: Both disorders share dopamine dysregulation, eye movement abnormalities, executive dysfunction and temporal lobe volume loss. Acetylcholine is not implicated.

questions.question_text: In this form of depression, somatic symptoms may be chief complaints, it is more common in the undeveloped world and mood is not always the chief complaint. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Masked depression presents with somatic complaints rather than explicit low mood and is more frequently reported in some cultures.

questions.question_text: Dialectical behavioural therapy was developed for borderline personality disorder. Which is not a core component?
questions.explanation: DBT core components are dialectical thinking, mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness, not analysis of communication.

questions.question_text: The CAMDEX includes all the following, except which one?
questions.explanation: CAMDEX incorporates the MMSE, Blessed scale, NART and other cognitive tests; the Tower of London is not included.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man with Parkinson’s disease on dopamine agonists may develop which hallucinations?
questions.explanation: Visual hallucinations are the most common with dopamine agonist therapy in Parkinson’s disease.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old with first-episode psychosis, abrupt onset, paranoid symptoms, no negatives, family history of mood disorder, unmarried. Which is a negative prognostic factor?
questions.explanation: Being unmarried is associated with poorer social support and is a negative prognostic factor in schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Which intervention is most appropriate for a man dependent on alcohol but in the contemplation stage of change?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing is the recommended approach for patients who are ambivalent about change (contemplation).

questions.question_text: Which statement about Rett syndrome is incorrect?

options.text: The incidence of sudden and unexpected death is usually around 5%.
The condition has been predominantly a female disorder.
The deterioration usually occurs between 7 and 24 months.
Anticonvulsant treatment is helpful with seizure control.
Behaviour therapy is helpful for controlling self-injurious behaviour.

correct_answer.text: The incidence of sudden and unexpected death is usually around 5%.

correct_answers.text: The incidence of sudden and unexpected death is usually around 5%.

questions.explanation: Sudden and unexpected death occurs in about 2% of Rett syndrome cases, not 5%.

questions.question_text: Childhood disintegrative disorder: normal development occurs for up to how many years after birth?
questions.explanation: Childhood disintegrative disorder features normal development for at least 2 years, with subsequent marked regression.

questions.question_text: To diagnose Tourette’s syndrome, the first symptom to appear is usually:
questions.explanation: Simple motor tics (e.g. blinking, grimacing) are typically the initial signs of Tourette’s syndrome.

questions.question_text: The Connors’ rating scale for ADHD includes all the following components except:
questions.explanation: The Connors’ scale measures ADHD behaviours, cognitive problems, anxiety, oppositional and social issues; it does not include a separate depression scale.

questions.question_text: What is the relapse rate for non-psychotic depression for those who have had one prior episode of postpartum depression?
questions.explanation: The relapse rate for subsequent non-psychotic depression after one episode of postpartum depression is about one in six.

questions.question_text: The risk of psychosis recurring in a subsequent pregnancy after one episode of postpartum psychosis has been estimated to be:
questions.explanation: The recurrence risk of postpartum psychosis in a subsequent pregnancy is approximately one in three.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the usage of psychotropic medications in breastfeeding is incorrect?

options.text: For bipolar disorder, valproate can be used, but the mother should be advised to ensure adequate contraception to prevent pregnancy.
For bipolar disorder, lithium, at low doses, can be used and is safe for neonates.
For depressive disorder, the recommended medications are paroxetine and sertraline.
For schizophrenia, only olanzapine and sulpiride have been recommended.
Methadone is not contraindicated for usage in mothers who are breastfeeding.

correct_answer.text: For bipolar disorder, lithium, at low doses, can be used and is safe for neonates.

correct_answers.text: For bipolar disorder, lithium, at low doses, can be used and is safe for neonates.

questions.explanation: Lithium carries risks to the breastfed infant and requires close monitoring; it is not universally considered safe at low doses.

questions.question_text: Extended Match Item 111: He denies being depressed and evades questions about the amputation.
questions.explanation: Denial is the refusal to acknowledge an unpleasant reality or feeling.

questions.question_text: Extended Match Item 112: He becomes angry with the psychiatrist, accusing him of making his mood worse.
questions.explanation: Projection involves attributing one’s own unacceptable impulses or feelings onto another person.

questions.question_text: Extended Match Item 113: At home, he scolds his wife badly for a trivial matter after hearing colleagues’ comments.
questions.explanation: Displacement is the transfer of emotions from a threatening object to a safer substitute.

questions.question_text: Extended Match Item 114: Two months later he volunteers to support disabled people, feeling better.
questions.explanation: Sublimation channels unacceptable impulses into socially constructive activities, such as volunteering.

questions.question_text: The nurse asks her to change out of her own clothing and wear hospital attire. She becomes upset and tries to hit the nurse. During a psychotherapy session, she realizes that her desire to hit the nurse was related to her father hitting her when she was a child.
questions.explanation: Acting out is enacting an unconscious wish or fantasy impulsively as a way of avoiding painful affect. In this case, the patient expresses her unconscious emotional conflicts and feelings regarding her father and the physical abuse directly through hitting the nurse, without being consciously aware of the meaning.

questions.question_text: She mentions that she has been trying to block memories about her past abuse from entering her mind.
questions.explanation: Suppression refers to the conscious effort not to attend to certain feelings or impulses, while repression refers to the blockage or expulsion of unacceptable ideas or impulses in the inner states to stop them from entering consciousness. In this case, the patient consciously makes an attempt to block her memories of the past so as not to affect her mood.

questions.question_text: She says that she cut herself on the arm with a penknife to externalize her pain and ease her stress in life. She feels that self‐cutting is an acceptable way of coping and that it has benefits in making her mind clearer and stabilizing her emotions.
questions.explanation: Rationalization refers to the justification of unacceptable attitudes, beliefs or behaviours, making them tolerable to oneself. In this case, the patient tries to justify and explain her rationale for self‐cutting, which she perceives as an acceptable way of coping with her emotions.

questions.question_text: She refers to abstract philosophy to explain her current plight.
questions.explanation: Intellectualization refers to the excessive use of abstract ideation to avoid difficult feelings or conflicts. In this case, the patient uses abstract thinking to explain her situation, and this in turn prevents her from facing her inner conflicts and feelings.

questions.question_text: After speaking to the ward doctor for 20 min, she believes that he is the best doctor she has ever seen. She demands to be seen only by the ward doctor.
questions.explanation: Idealization refers to attributing perfect or near-perfect qualities onto others as a way of avoiding negative feelings. In this case, the patient idealizes the doctor despite having only seen him once, and she has strong positive feelings towards him.

questions.question_text: She is noted to be lying flat on the floor, clutching a teddy bear and crying loudly. When the nurse asks what happened, she replies, in a child‐like manner, that the other patients bullied her.
questions.explanation: In regression, there is a transition, at times of stress and threat, to modes of functioning that are of a lower level of complexity so that one returns to an earlier level of maturational functioning. In this case, the patient acts in a childlike manner when the stress becomes overwhelming.

questions.question_text: Her brother mentions that she had tried to separate herself from her emotions ever since her aunt, with whom she was close, passed away a few months ago.
questions.explanation: Isolation of affect refers to the separation of an idea from its associated affect to avoid emotional pain. By doing this, the patient’s link with the unhappy thoughts and memories is broken.

questions.question_text: She tries to take on the quality of her aunt, who had passed away a few months ago, by behaving like her.
questions.explanation: Identification refers to internalization of the qualities of another person by behaving like that person. In this case, the patient takes on the qualities of her aunt by behaving like her.

questions.question_text: A study was conducted to evaluate the effects of antidepressants on immunological function. Thirty depressed patients were treated with SSRIs and placebo in a crossover design with a wash‐out period in between. Cytokine levels were measured during treatment and placebo.
questions.explanation: The Kruskal–Wallis test is a distribution‐free method that is the analogue of the ANOVA of a one‐way design, used to test whether a series of populations have the same median.

questions.question_text: A researcher wants to find out which type of antidepressants (tricyclic antidepressants, SSRIs and serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) leads to better quality of life in depressed patients. The patients fill up SF‐36, which assesses their health‐related quality of life, and the doctor independently assesses the global assessment of functioning (GAF) score. Both SF‐36 and GAF scores are normally distributed. The researcher will compare the SF‐36 and GAF scores of patients receiving the three types of antidepressants.
questions.explanation: ANOVA separates variation attributable to one factor from that attributable to others. In a one‐way design, it compares means of more than two groups on a normally distributed dependent variable.

questions.question_text: In an undergraduate examination that follows the closed marking system (candidates usually score between 4 and 7, where 4 = fail, 5 = pass, 7 = distinction), the chief examiner wants to compare the median examination score between local and immigrant doctors.
questions.explanation: The two‐way ANOVA extends one‐way ANOVA when more than one independent variable is involved and multiple observations exist for each factor level.

questions.question_text: Case series.
questions.explanation: According to the CEBM hierarchy, case series are classified as level 4 evidence.

questions.question_text: Ecological studies.
questions.explanation: Ecological studies fall under level 2C evidence in the hierarchy of research evidence.

questions.question_text: Expert opinion.
questions.explanation: Expert opinion without explicit critical appraisal is considered level 5 evidence.

questions.question_text: Mild learning disability.
questions.explanation: About 85 % of individuals with learning disability have mild mental retardation (IQ 50–69), so approximately 60 % fall into the mild category.

questions.question_text: Moderate learning disability.
questions.explanation: Moderate mental retardation (IQ 35–49) accounts for about 10 % of those with learning disability.

questions.question_text: Severe learning disability.
questions.explanation: Severe mental retardation (IQ 20–34) represents about 3 % of the learning‐disabled population.

questions.question_text: Profound learning disability.
questions.explanation: Profound mental retardation (IQ < 20) accounts for approximately 2 % of those with learning disability.

questions.question_text: Which of the following are considered as standardized instruments for formal cognitive testing? (Choose four options.)

options.text: Dementia questionnaire for the mentally retarded

questions.explanation: Standardized instruments for formal cognitive testing include the MMSE, Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Assessment Revised, Montreal Cognitive Assessment and Clinical Dementia Rating Scale.

questions.question_text: Which two of the above could be used for assessment of cognition for those with learning disabilities? (Choose two options.)

options.text: Dementia questionnaire for the mentally retarded

correct_answer.text: Dementia questionnaire for the mentally retarded

correct_answers.text: Dementia questionnaire for the mentally retarded

questions.explanation: For those with learning disabilities, the Dementia Questionnaire for the Mentally Retarded and the Dementia Scale for Down Syndrome are appropriate assessment tools.

questions.question_text: The CAMDEX includes which of the above questionnaires? (Choose six options.)

options.text: Dementia questionnaire for the mentally retarded

questions.explanation: The CAMDEX includes the MMSE, Blessed Dementia Rating Scale, Hachinski Ischaemic Score, NART, Kendrick Object Learning Test and Wisconsin Card Sorting Test.

questions.question_text: Which one of the above is one of the classical findings in Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD)? (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Gross atrophy in fronto-temporal regions (knife-blade atrophy) is a classical finding in Pick disease rather than CJD. CJD is diagnosed by EEG and clinical features.

questions.question_text: Which one is a classical neuro-imaging finding for frontotemporal dementia? (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Anterior hypo-perfusion on functional imaging is characteristic of frontotemporal dementia.

questions.question_text: Which two are characteristic findings for vascular dementia? (Choose two options.)
questions.explanation: Vascular dementia is characterized by subcortical vascular encephalopathy and small well-localized subcortical infarcts on imaging.

questions.question_text: Which two of the above are classical imaging findings for individuals with Alzheimer’s dementia? (Choose two options.)
questions.explanation: Alzheimer’s dementia typically shows cortical atrophy with ventricular enlargement and hippocampal atrophy on imaging.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman with no medical history of note presents with sudden onset of blindness following the death of her mother. She is reviewed by both the neurologist and the ophthalmologist, but no physical cause is found for her symptoms.
questions.explanation: This presentation is consistent with conversion disorder, where psychological conflict is unconsciously converted into a neurological symptom without organic pathology.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man presents to the hospital complaining of abdominal pain and haemoptysis. He demands admission. He undergoes colonoscopy and blood investigations, which were all normal. He self-discharges when given the results of the investigations. This is his tenth admission in 8 months, each admission resulting in self-discharge.
questions.explanation: Factitious disorder (Munchausen syndrome) involves intentional production of symptoms for the sick role, often resulting in peregrination and repeated admissions.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman comes to the hospital complaining of severe headache. She is very worried that she has a severe brain condition that will make her lose her mind. Her grandmother passed away from a brain tumour a few years ago. Despite repeated normal brain scans and reassurance from the doctors, she is not totally convinced. She decides to seek a consultation from another doctor, as she is concerned that her current doctor could have missed a serious medical condition causing her headache.
questions.explanation: Hypochondriasis is characterized by an intense fear of serious illness despite normal investigations and reassurance.

questions.question_text: A 17-year-old woman comes to the emergency department complaining of leg pain. She is noted to be joking with the friends who accompanied her, but she becomes tearful and demands to be given a sick note to rest at home when the doctor comes to review her. Her history and physical examination are inconsistent, and investigations are unremarkable. A staff nurse overhears the patient telling her friends that she is planning to go on a holiday for the next 3 days.
questions.explanation: Malingering involves intentional production of symptoms for external gain (e.g., a sick note and time off for a holiday).

questions.question_text: Verbal aggression.
questions.explanation: Among outpatients with schizophrenia, verbal aggression occurs in approximately 45% of cases.

questions.question_text: Physical violence towards objects.
questions.explanation: Physical violence towards objects is seen in about 29% (approximately 30%) of patients with schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Physical violence towards others.
questions.explanation: Physical violence towards others is observed in roughly 19% to 20% of schizophrenia outpatients.

questions.question_text: Self‐directed violence.
questions.explanation: Self‐directed violence (suicidal or self‐harm behavior) occurs in about 8% to 10% of patients with schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Family members involved in the assaults.
questions.explanation: About 50% of assaults by patients with schizophrenia are directed towards family members.

questions.question_text: Strangers being attacked in the assaults.
questions.explanation: Strangers are attacked in about 20% of violent incidents involving patients with schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: A 79-year-old man with right-sided hemiparesis presents with sudden episodes of uncontrollable crying.
questions.explanation: Emotionalism (pathological laughing or crying) is characterized by uncontrollable episodes of crying or laughing following a stroke, often with preserved mood congruence.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old woman with left opercular lesions presents with aggression and emotional outbursts when she is unable to express herself using language.
questions.explanation: Catastrophic reaction is a sudden emotional outburst (aggression or crying) seen in patients with expressive aphasia due to left opercular lesions when they cannot communicate.

questions.question_text: A 73-year-old man with lacunar infarcts presents with hemiparesis, dysphasia, depression and cognitive impairment.
questions.explanation: Vascular dementia presents with focal neurological signs (e.g. hemiparesis, dysphasia) in addition to cognitive decline and depression.

questions.question_text: A 68-year-old woman with a vascular insult to the basal ganglia presents with feelings of hopelessness, anhedonia, psychomotor retardation and hypersomnia.
questions.explanation: Depression is common after stroke, especially with basal ganglia lesions, and presents with typical mood and sleep disturbances.

questions.question_text: If the mother develops a relapse of bipolar disorder immediately after pregnancy, which one of the commonly used mood stabilizers should not be used in view of her intending to still breastfeed her child?
questions.explanation: Lithium is contraindicated in breastfeeding due to risk of neonatal toxicity; valproate is preferred with contraception advice.

questions.question_text: If the mother is depressed after pregnancy, which of the commonly used antidepressants could be used, if she is still keen to breastfeed her child?
questions.explanation: Paroxetine and sertraline have low levels in breast milk and are recommended for breastfeeding mothers with depression.

questions.question_text: If the mother is psychotic after pregnancy, which one of the commonly used antipsychotics should be avoided, in view of the fact that she is actively breastfeeding her child?
questions.explanation: Clozapine should be avoided in breastfeeding mothers due to high risk of agranulocytosis in the infant.

questions.question_text: Which medication is suitable for mothers who are using substances but who also want to breastfeed their newborn?
questions.explanation: Methadone is compatible with breastfeeding when doses are kept as low as possible.

questions.question_text: Which antipsychotic medications are not indicated? (Choose two options.)
questions.explanation: Clozapine and olanzapine are not indicated in patients with atrial fibrillation; aripiprazole is the preferred antipsychotic in this setting.

questions.question_text: Which antidepressant is safe for use in patients with atrial fibrillation?
questions.explanation: Mirtazapine is often used safely in patients with atrial fibrillation on anticoagulants and does not adversely affect heart rhythm.

questions.question_text: Which mood stabilizers are safe for use in patients with atrial fibrillation? (Choose two options.)
questions.explanation: Lithium and valproate are safe mood stabilizers in patients with atrial fibrillation.

questions.question_text: Which medication for dementia is safe for patients with atrial fibrillation?
questions.explanation: Rivastigmine is the safest acetylcholinesterase inhibitor for dementia in patients with atrial fibrillation.

questions.question_text: It indicates whether the measurement being assessed is superior to other measurements in approaching true validity.
questions.explanation: Incremental validity refers to the extent to which a new measure adds predictive power beyond existing measures.

questions.question_text: It examines whether the specific measurements aimed for by the measuring instrument are assessing the content of the measurement in question.
questions.explanation: Content validity assesses whether a test covers the full range of the concept it intends to measure.

questions.question_text: It compares the measure being assessed with an external valid yardstick at the same time.
questions.explanation: Concurrent validity evaluates how well a new test correlates with an established test measured at the same time.

questions.question_text: Ask the subject to recommend acquaintances who meet the sample criteria.
questions.explanation: Snowball sampling involves participants referring others who meet the study criteria.

questions.question_text: Subjects are chosen on basis of being readily available.
questions.explanation: Convenience sampling selects participants who are easiest to recruit.

questions.question_text: Assign members of the population into relatively homogeneous subgroups (strata) before sampling. Then, draw random sample of subjects from within each strata.
questions.explanation: Stratified sampling divides the population into strata and then randomly samples from each.

questions.question_text: Concepts of projective identification and splitting in borderline personality disorder.
questions.explanation: Melanie Klein introduced the concepts of splitting and projective identification in object relations theory.

questions.question_text: Archetypes are representations of experiences in the collective unconscious that lead to conflicts and anxiety.
questions.explanation: Carl Jung described archetypes as universal symbols in the collective unconscious.

questions.question_text: Ocnophil (clingy and dependent) and philobat (grandiose and pseudo‐independent) are two types of defensive strategies against separation anxiety.
questions.explanation: Michael Balint coined the terms ocnophil and philobat to describe defensive patterns against separation anxiety.

questions.question_text: Autistic phase, symbiosis, separation‐individuation.
questions.explanation: Margaret Mahler described the separation‐individuation process in early child development.

questions.question_text: The therapist acts as container for the client’s projections for exploration of feelings.
questions.explanation: Wilfred Bion emphasized the therapist’s function as container for the patient’s projected feelings.

questions.question_text: Internal world is a substitute for a frustrating experience in external relationships and frustration often leads to aggression.
questions.explanation: Ronald Fairbairn’s object relations theory highlights how internal object relations replace frustrating external relationships.

questions.question_text: A good‐enough mother helps the child to progress from dependency to independence.
questions.explanation: Donald Winnicott introduced the concept of the good‐enough mother in supporting healthy child development.

questions.question_text: Classified attachment based on the adult attachment interview into autonomous attachment, dismissive attachment, preoccupied attachment.
questions.explanation: John Bowlby developed attachment theory and classified adult attachment styles using the AAI.

questions.question_text: Concept of self‐psychology where self has a central and functional role in the mind.
questions.explanation: Heinz Kohut founded self‐psychology, emphasizing the central role of the self in mental life.

questions.question_text: The main neurochemical effect is via the blockage of N‐methyl‐D‐aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptors.
questions.explanation: Phencyclidine (PCP) is a dissociative drug that blocks NMDA glutamate receptors.

questions.question_text: The mechanism of action of this particular drug of abuse is via serotonin neurotoxin.
questions.explanation: MDMA is a serotonin neurotoxin, causing release and depletion of serotonin.

questions.question_text: This leads to the activation of particular receptors, and this would inhibit adenylate cyclase.
questions.explanation: Cannabis activates CB1 and CB2 receptors, which are coupled to inhibitory G‐proteins that reduce adenylate cyclase activity.

questions.question_text: The binding of this particular drug to the mu receptors inhibits the release of GABA from the nerve terminal and thus reduces the inhibitory effect of GABA on dopaminergic neurons.
questions.explanation: Opioids bind to mu receptors, inhibiting GABA release and disinhibiting dopaminergic neurons.

questions.question_text: In this form of prevention, it involves the reduction of birth‐related trauma as well as the prevention of infection and the prevention of neural tube defects by taking folate during pregnancy.
questions.explanation: Primary prevention aims to prevent disease before it occurs, including folate supplementation and infection control.

questions.question_text: This involves typically active resettlement programs with expansion of support networks.
questions.explanation: Tertiary prevention focuses on managing disease and preventing complications, such as community support and resettlement.

questions.question_text: This involves typically prenatal diagnosis and maternal serum alpha foetoprotein screening.
questions.explanation: Secondary prevention seeks to detect disease early, for example via prenatal screening.

questions.question_text: A mother who has one child with autism is currently expecting her second child. What is the estimated risk of her second child developing autism?
questions.explanation: The recurrence risk for narrowly defined autism in siblings is approximately 3%.

questions.question_text: A 12-year-old has been previously diagnosed with Tourette’s syndrome. What is the estimated probability that he might have Asperger’s syndrome as a comorbid?
questions.explanation: About 10% of children with Tourette’s syndrome have comorbid Asperger’s syndrome.

questions.question_text: An 80-year-old man presents with fluctuating, progressive memory loss and emotional incontinence. He has history of falls and is being treated for hypertension by his GP. His relatives say that his personality is preserved.
questions.explanation: Vascular dementia presents with stepwise decline, fluctuating cognition, pseudobulbar affect, and vascular risk factors.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old woman presents with memory loss following the death of her husband 4 months ago. She also complains of poor sleep, lack of energy and weight loss. During the cognitive assessment, she is not keen to answer the questions.
questions.explanation: Pseudodementia due to depression mimics cognitive decline but is related to mood and lack of motivation.

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old man presents with cognitive impairment and fluctuating levels of consciousness, particularly confusion and bizarre behaviour in the evenings. His daughter claims that he has been seeing ghosts and not able to turn in his bed. On physical examination, he is found to have hypertonia and hypersalivation. The score on MMSE is 15/30. These above symptoms worsen following the commencement of antipsychotic medication.
questions.explanation: Lewy body dementia presents with visual hallucinations, fluctuating consciousness, parkinsonism and sensitivity to antipsychotics.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman presents with a cognitive deterioration and mood changes. On physical examination, there are gait abnormalities. She has a past medical history of epilepsy and migraines with aura. She also has episodes of left-sided muscular weakness. On further inquiry, her aunt has similar problems.
questions.explanation: CADASIL is an autosomal dominant leukoencephalopathy causing stroke-like episodes, migraine auras and cognitive decline.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old woman was found wandering on the streets with some memory loss after the recent funeral of her husband. She was brought in by the police for psychiatric assessment. When you assess her, she is unable to recall her personal details. She is physically well, and all investigations are normal.
questions.explanation: Psychogenic fugue involves dissociative amnesia with travel and loss of personal identity in the absence of organic pathology.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man who was previously a reserved and religious teacher began making out-of-character remarks, talking aloud about pornography and talking to strangers in the bus stop. He has been aggressive to his wife. When you ask him a new question, he gives you the answers to the previous questions.
questions.explanation: Frontal lobe dementia is marked by personality change, disinhibition and executive dysfunction.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old woman with chronic hypertension presents with gradual reduction in memory, step-like intellectual decline and slowness in motor functions. MRI shows periventricular lucencies, multiple microvascular infarcts in areas supplied by perforating vessels and white matter leukoaraiosis. SPECT scan shows bilateral reduction of blood flow in thalamus, basal ganglia and frontal lobes.
questions.explanation: Binswanger’s disease is a subcortical vascular encephalopathy with white matter changes and multiple lacunar infarcts.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman who is 10 weeks’ pregnant was admitted to the obstetric ward after excessive vomiting. She has very poor oral intake and was given intravenous dextrose solution for fluid replacement. Subsequently, she develops memory problems. Neurological examination reveals horizontal diplopia and ataxia. Her husband mentions that she does not drink alcohol.
questions.explanation: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency (Wernicke’s encephalopathy) presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion.
